newsitem.title: UK: Bosnians warned economic aid won't last forever.
newsitem.headline: Bosnians warned economic aid won't last forever.

text.p: The international community will tell Bosnia it has to gradually cut its dependence on foreign aid and take responsibility for its own economy, British officials said on Tuesday.
They said the message would be spelled out at a two-day conference to review the Bosnia peace process which opens in London on Wednesday.

But some international banking sources were sceptical, arguing privately that it was pointless to talk about issues like creating a Bosnian central bank when the ravaged country did not have an effective central government.
"The need for the authorities of Bosnia Herzegovina to take the lead, and take responsibility for their own reconstruction, is very, very important," a British official told a news briefing.
"We need to move from reconstruction to economic development...the international community doesn't want to be there forever."

He said that by the end of next year the West would want to see Bosnia start to resemble countries like Romania, Poland and Hungary and was also eager to see a central bank set up to facilitate reconstruction and debt negotiation.
"By the end of 1997 we will begin to see something much more like the eastern Europe situation," he added.

Earlier this year the World Bank estimated Bosnia needed some $5.1 billion for reconstruction by the end of the century, and in April international donors pledged some $1.8 billion for urgent rebuilding in 1996 alone.
One British official said estimates showed that most of the amount pledged for 1996 had been spent, though a second donors' conference will have to be held, probably in February next year.
Agencies like the World Bank, the European Union and the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) have spearheaded the reconstruction drive, but critics say the pace has been too slow.
In truth, the level of mistrust in the Balkan state has hampered efforts to rebuild the country.

Donors have been reluctant to send aid to help rebuild Bosnia's Serb republic because of its failure to comply in full with the terms of last year's Dayton peace agreement that ended the 43-month war.
It has taken more than two months to agree on a structure for the country's national government, prompting some observers to argue that it is too soon to be talking about setting up a market economy.
"The reconstruction issues will be somewhat in the background -- the key thing is we still haven't got a (working) government," said one international banker close to the peace process.
"Reconstruction will be more important as we get closer on the political issues -- until then we are marking time."
But Josue Tanaka, director of the EBRD's country team for Bosnia, said this made reconstruction all the more vital.

"To a certain extent we can achieve results on the economic side that contribute to reducing the pressure on the political side," he said by telephone. "My perception is one has to try to cement the situation as much as we can."
